R, the language in which the workshop's analysis is written, is presented in this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) as it is used in the Europeanisation and the economy case study. The first steps in R, from the console and the script to objects, data frames, the pipe, the datawizard verbs, a first table and a first figure, are taught in [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html) on the workshop's umbrella site, a module that assumes no programming at all and works on a file small enough to be examined whole, with an outcome that is either yes or no. Assuming those steps, this page applies the tools to the country-year panel of the Europeanisation case study, a table of 270 rows built from Eurobarometer surveys, covering the files of the case study and the routes by which they arrive, the grammar of graphics in depth, and the specification curve of the case study.

The panel provides the material for two things that a file of yes-or-no outcomes cannot show. A scatterplot with a fitted line needs measures that vary continuously, which the panel contains, among them the unemployment rate and the mean score with which the respondents of a country-year framed the EU in cosmopolitan terms. The curve of the case study, for its part, combines predictors whose results point in opposite directions, and therefore has to be aligned with the claim before it can be read.

The code of sections 2 and 3 is shown without being run, because it reads the panel of the case study, which is on your machine once you have the workspace, and the numbers quoted in section 3 are computed from the curve of the case study when the page is built. Typing the code yourself, however, remains the way to learn. Copy each block into the workspace and run it there.

## 1. Other formats, and fetching data {#sec-formats}

The panel and the curve of the case study are CSV files, read in the same way as the file of [section 6 of Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-reading). The Eurobarometer waves from which the panel was built are supplied by the GESIS archive in another format, that of the statistical package Stata, with value labels on their answer codes. [Section 13](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r-further.html#sec-formats) of the second part of that module reads a file of this kind in the browser, with its labels, and also covers the other formats in which data arrive, from Excel workbooks to Parquet files. In the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-build), the respondent file of this case study is built from the Stata files of the waves.

The data of the case study arrive by three routes, for each of which the [subsection on fetching data](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r-further.html#sec-fetching) in the same part introduces the corresponding package. The panel is fetched from the Open Science Framework by the script `R/get_data.R` in the workspace of the case study, a script that uses the osfr package. The macro variables of the panel were obtained from the World Bank with the WDI package, which queries the indicators of the World Bank by their codes, as described in [section 3.2](data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank) of the data sources module. The Eurobarometer waves come from the GESIS archive, which offers no interface through which a program could download them, and the workshop therefore downloads the waves by hand, as shown step by step in [section 3.1](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) of the same module.

## 2. The grammar of graphics {#sec-grammar}

[Section 12 of Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-figure) draws a first figure, and this section develops the grammar further on the panel of the Europeanisation case study, read as `europeanisation <- readr::read_csv("data/europeanisation_cy.csv")` in the workspace of the case study. Its 270 rows correspond to 27 countries in each of ten years, and its columns include the unemployment rate (`unemp`), the mean score of cosmopolitan framing of the EU among the respondents of each country-year (`mcosmo`, from 0 to 1) and whether an EU or IMF assistance programme was running (`bailout`), the panel thus containing the continuous measures that a scatterplot, a fitted line and a panel for each country need. It is **ggplot2**, a member of the tidyverse family of packages, that draws such figures [@WickhamEtAl2019WelcomeTidyverse]. As almost every chart on the workshop's pages and slides is built with it, reading ggplot2 code is how you satisfy yourself that a figure shows what its caption says it shows. The figures that you draw yourself, in the workspaces and the browser labs, and the live class chart on the Class results page of the case study, are drawn with tinyplot ([section 12 of Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-figure)), which is light enough to run in a browser. The other exceptions are the main chart of the [Specification curve page](../curve.qmd) of the Europeanisation case study, drawn in the browser by one of the workshop's scripts, the charts of the [decision map](../menu.qmd#map), drawn by Observable Plot, and a few figures in the methods modules, drawn by packages with plotting functions of their own.

The name of the package abbreviates 'the grammar of graphics', the idea that any chart can be described as a combination of a few standard parts, much as a grammar describes how words combine into sentences. ggplot2 therefore has no separate function for each chart type, splitting a figure instead into parts that recombine freely: the data, the mapping from columns to visual properties, the geometric shapes drawn, the scales that decide what those shapes look like, the panels that the plot is divided into, and last the labels and the styling. A scatterplot and a bar chart are two fillings of the same slots, and once you know the slots you can read the figures on the workshop's website, including kinds you have not met yet.

### Data, mapping and geometry

A plot needs data, a mapping and at least one geom, while everything else has a default good enough to start with.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()
```

Three things happen there. `ggplot()` receives the data frame and declares which columns drive the picture. `aes()` is the **aesthetic mapping**, and it states that the unemployment rate governs horizontal position while the cosmopolitan-framing score governs vertical position. `geom_point()` adds a **geom**, a layer of geometric shapes, drawing one point per row – 270 points for 270 country-years. Axis ranges, tick marks, gridlines and the panel background are all inferred from the data, which is why this bare version is already a readable figure.

Layers are joined with `+`, never with the pipe `|>`, for a historical reason, since ggplot2 settled on `+` years before R had a native pipe. The practical consequence is that a long chain changes operator exactly once, at the point where it stops reshaping data and starts drawing, and typing `|>` where `+` belongs is among the commonest first-week errors in R.

### Mapping and setting

Every visual property of a layer can be specified in two ways, and confusing the two is the next commonest error. Put a property inside `aes()` and it is **mapped**: its value is read from a column, it varies row by row, and ggplot2 adds a legend explaining the correspondence. Put the same property outside `aes()`, as an ordinary argument to the geom, and it is **set**, taking one fixed value for the whole layer, with no legend because there is nothing to explain.

```r
# MAPPED: colour comes from a column, so the points differ and a legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()

# SET: colour is a constant, identical for every point, and no legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.5)
```

`alpha` controls opacity, running from 0 for invisible to 1 for solid, and setting it below 1 is the standard remedy for a scatterplot in which points pile up on one another. The constant `"#0e3b6a"` is a hex colour code, the dark blue used in the workshop's figures.

Leaving out the `factor()` wrapped around `bailout` produces the wrong figure without any warning. Since `bailout` is stored as 0 and 1 in numeric form, `colour = bailout` gives ggplot2 a number, which it treats as continuous, drawing a colour gradient and a legend running smoothly from 0.00 to 1.00. What you wanted was two categories in two colours, and `factor(bailout)` is how you say so. The same applies to `year`, which is also numeric: map it raw for a gradient across the decade, or wrap it in `factor()` for ten discrete groups.

### Layers

A figure can have as many layers as you need, each with its own geom, drawn in the order in which they are written, with later layers covering earlier ones.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15)
```

The grey points are drawn first and the trend line over them. `geom_smooth()` fits a line through the cloud and draws it with a band showing the uncertainty around it, and `method = "lm"` asks for a straight line from the same least-squares method used in the module on panel data to fit models. R then prints the message `` `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``, which only reports the relationship that was fitted and needs no action. Reference layers behave in the same way, `geom_hline(yintercept = 0)` ruling a horizontal line at zero of the kind used in section 3 to divide a figure into results that support a claim and results that do not.

Line thickness is set with `linewidth`, whereas point size and type size are set with `size`, and confusion between the two lies behind a great many warnings.

```r
ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.4)   # the thickness of a drawn line
ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7)       # the area of a plotted point
ggplot2::geom_text(size = 3.5)        # the height of a piece of type
```

Passing `size` to a line geom still works, but R warns "Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. Please use `linewidth` instead." The two names survive side by side because `size` on a point means an area and on text a height, neither of which is a line thickness.

### Scales

The mapping states which column drives colour, while the **scale** decides which colours it drives, and the same applies to positions, sizes and shapes. Every mapping receives a default scale, and you override it whenever the default is not what a reader needs.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    name   = "Assistance programme",
    values = c("0" = "#848c94", "1" = "#a10000"),
    labels = c("0" = "none", "1" = "bailout")
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5))
```

`scale_colour_manual()` names a colour for each level of the variable. Giving `values` and `labels` as *named* vectors, with `"0" = …` rather than a bare pair, means that the assignment cannot silently reverse itself if the data ever arrives in a different order. The workshop's colours are defined once, in `style/cgm-slides.scss`, with an orange and a green drawn from a palette built to stay distinguishable under the commonest forms of colour vision deficiency.

Position scales follow the same logic of overriding a default, and one of their arguments catches people out. `scale_x_continuous(breaks = …)` decides where the tick marks fall, but the sibling argument `limits` **removes** every row outside the range before any statistic is computed, leaving a smoother to be refitted on whatever rows remain.

```r
p_trend <- ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a")

p_trend + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.30, 0.50))   # drops rows, then refits
p_trend + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.30, 0.50))        # keeps every row, only zooms
```

Run the first of those and R warns "Removed 163 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`)", and the trend line you are looking at now runs through 107 country-years rather than 270. `coord_cartesian()`, by contrast, zooms the finished figure and leaves the computation untouched, which makes it the function to use when you only want a closer look.

### Facets

**Faceting** repeats the same plot once per group, on shared axes, so that the groups can be compared by eye rather than by disentangling overlapping series. A country-year table lends itself well to faceting, since each country can have a panel of its own.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013))
```

Twenty-seven small panels appear, one per country code, each showing the cosmopolitan-framing series of that country across the decade. In the browser lab of the Europeanisation case study the same figure is drawn with tinyplot early in the exercise, so that the crisis years are in view before any model is fitted and it is plain how differently the countries move. The `~ cntry` is a one-sided formula, with nothing to the left of the `~`, whereas a model formula, as in `lm()`, uses the same syntax with an outcome written on the left. `ncol` fixes the shape of the grid, and where two grouping variables matter, `facet_grid(rows = vars(a), cols = vars(b))` crosses them into a matrix of panels.

### Labels and themes

Two layers finish a figure. `labs()` supplies the words – axis titles, plot title, subtitle, caption, legend name – and it deserves more care than beginners give it, because a column name such as `mcosmo` means nothing to a reader who has not opened the codebook. The **theme** then governs everything with no data behind it: type size, gridlines, background, the position of the legend.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x       = "Unemployment rate (%)",
    y       = "Cosmopolitan framing (mean score, 0–1)",
    title   = "Unemployment and cosmopolitan framing",
    caption = "270 country-years, europeanisation_cy.csv"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    plot.title       = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )
```

`theme_minimal()` is the default look across the workshop, and `base_size` is its most useful argument, scaling every piece of type at once: 9 for a dense panel of small multiples, 12 for a page figure, 15 and upwards for a slide. A bare `theme()` afterwards overrides individual pieces, and the order matters, because a complete theme applied *after* your adjustments would wipe them out. Inside it, `element_blank()` deletes a piece outright, `element_text()` restyles type, and `element_line()` restyles rules and gridlines.

As a plot is an ordinary R object, you can store it under a name, extend it later and write it to a file:

```r
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(europeanisation, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = "Cosmopolitan framing")

p + ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot2::ggsave("figures/framing_unemployment.png", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

`ggsave()` takes its dimensions in inches and writes whichever format the file extension names. When you do not name a plot, it saves the last one drawn, which is convenient but can save the wrong figure, so name the object.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Draw the scatterplot of `unemp` against `mcosmo`, then change one thing at a time and watch what moves. Swap `geom_point()` for `geom_text(aes(label = cntry))` and each point becomes its country code; move `colour = factor(bailout)` from inside `aes()` to outside it and read the error it raises; drop the `factor()` and compare the two legends. Then add `facet_wrap(~ year)` and decide for yourself whether ten panels tell you more than one crowded cloud does.
:::

### From the pipe to the plot

Reshaping and drawing usually take place in one chain, with datawizard passing its result straight to ggplot2, the chain using `|>` while it is still working on data and switching to `+` once `ggplot()` appears.

```r
europeanisation |>
  datawizard::data_filter(year >= 2009) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(mean_unemp = mean(unemp), by = "cntry") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = reorder(cntry, mean_unemp), y = mean_unemp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean unemployment, 2009–2013 (%)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

`reorder()` sorts the country codes by the value being plotted rather than alphabetically, which turns a jumble of bars into a ranking you can read at a glance. `geom_col()` draws a bar whose height is the number stored in the data, which is what you want once `data_summary()` has already done the counting. Its cousin `geom_bar()`, by contrast, counts the rows for you, and reaching for the wrong one of the two is a frequent small frustration.

Where two figures belong side by side, the **patchwork** package composes whole plots. `patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)` sets two plot objects in a row, and `patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, nrow = 1)` does the same for a list of them, while with the package attached by `library(patchwork)`, `p1 + p2` does so with the same `+` that adds layers.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Build a chain that keeps the crisis years, groups by `year`, and reports the mean of `mcosmo` and the mean of `mneg` per year, then pipe it into a plot with two `geom_line()` layers in different colours. You will find yourself wanting a legend and not getting one, because both colours were set rather than mapped. The remedy is to reshape the data into long form, with one row per year and outcome, using `data_to_long()` from datawizard (or `pivot_longer()` from tidyr), and then to map `colour` to the column that names the outcome.
:::

## 3. Reading the specification curve {#sec-speccurve}

The workshop's central figure is a **specification curve**, and you now have every part needed to build one yourself. A hypothesis about a dataset admits many defensible analyses, and if you fit all of them and line the results up in order, you can see the range of answers that the data supports instead of the single answer that one analyst happened to report.

`data/spec_curve.csv` contains that curve for the Europeanisation case study: 864 rows, one per specification that the workshop judges a justifiable way of answering the claim, each recording the decisions that distinguish it from its neighbours, the partial correlation that it produced, and its p-values under several kinds of inference. The column `sig` records whether the p-value of a specification under standard errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom lies below 0.05, the test used in the workshop to class every point (explained in the [module on panel data](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference)), and `is_reference` marks the workshop's reference specification, the analysis submitted by analyst C6HJR to the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], one of the three analyses that Task 3 lets you choose to reproduce. Reading the file requires one preparatory step, explained in the paragraph after the code.

```r
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(r_ca = dplyr::if_else(predictor == "growth", -r, r)) |>   # claim alignment
  datawizard::data_arrange("r_ca") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n())

reference <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
```

The claim under test is that poor economic performance depresses the positive framing of the EU. With unemployment as the predictor, a negative correlation supports it, because a rise in unemployment is a worsening of the economy. With GDP growth as the predictor, support means a *positive* correlation instead, because a fall in growth is the worsening, and plotting the raw numbers together would scatter agreeing results on opposite sides of zero. **Claim alignment** repairs that by flipping the sign wherever the predictor is growth, after which a negative value means support for every row alike. `if_else()` performs the flip, and the `_ca` suffix is the workshop's naming habit for any claim-aligned quantity. As the file already contains the aligned value in a column of the same name, the line rebuilds something that you can check against the stored column. Sorting by the aligned value and numbering the rows then assigns each specification a rank, which becomes the horizontal axis.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(curve, ggplot2::aes(x = rank, y = r_ca)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = sig), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = reference, colour = "#8b1538", size = 3) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text",
    x = reference$rank, y = reference$r_ca - 0.08,
    label = "the reference specification\n(C6HJR, t = -3.804)",
    colour = "#8b1538", fontface = "bold", size = 3.2, hjust = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    name   = NULL,
    values = c("TRUE" = 1, "FALSE" = 4),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "CR2 p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "CR2 p ≥ 0.05")
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.65, 0.2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x     = "specification, ranked by claim-aligned partial correlation",
    y     = "claim-aligned partial correlation",
    title = "The curve of the claim"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Almost everything in that block has come up already: a reference line, a layer of small points whose shape is mapped to a logical column, a second point layer drawn from a *different* data frame, a manual scale, a zoom, labels and a theme. The manual scale establishes the convention used in the workshop's charts, an open circle for a result below the 5% threshold and a cross for one above it, drawn at the same size and in translucent ink so that dense stretches of the curve remain readable and the class of a point is read from its shape rather than from a colour. `data = reference` inside the geom overrides the frame given to `ggplot()`, and it is in this way that a single row is picked out and emphasised. `annotate()` is the one function that you have not met, adding a mark that comes from no column at all, since you supply the coordinates and the text yourself, which is why its position is read off `reference` rather than mapped.

Every point below the grey line is an analysis in the direction of the claim. Of the 864 specifications, 98.1% lie below it and 77.2% lie below it with a CR2 p-value under 0.05. The aligned correlations range from −0.589 to 0.116, the curve thus containing firm support and a few results on the other side of zero. The burgundy point is the reference specification, the analysis submitted by C6HJR to the robustness study, with a t-statistic of −3.804. Of the other specifications, 583 lie further below zero than it does, and with a CR2 p-value of 0.050 it is drawn as a cross. The submitted analysis appears to have been neither an outlier nor a cherry-pick, and yet the same menu, worked through in good faith by any competent analyst, would have produced a great many other numbers, most of them further in the direction of the claim.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Rebuild the curve, then add `colour = estimator` inside the `aes()` of the first point layer and delete the fixed `colour = "#0e3b6a"` that follows it, keeping the shapes as they are. The two colours largely separate along the ranking, which is why the estimator is the decision that moves the curve most, and the [Specification curve page](../curve.qmd) explains what the two designs compare. Then try `ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ predictor)` on the same figure and ask yourself which of the two pictures you would rather a reviewer saw.
:::

## Sources and further study {#sec-sources}

The open resources for a fuller grounding in R are listed under [further study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-sources) in Getting started with R. For the grammar of graphics, the chapters on visualisation in **"R for Data Science"**, the free book written by the authors of the tidyverse packages, at <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/>, cover ggplot2 in full, and the documentation of the package, at [ggplot2.tidyverse.org](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), is readable as an introduction as well as a reference.

When you are ready for a first statistical model, the module on [panel data](panel-data.qmd) extends the linear model to the panel models required by the Europeanisation case study.
